title: SongSketch AnyKey
user: A young or returning browser-based songwriter who wants to sketch an any-length melody and drums without being locked to a scale or installing a DAW.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent asks for a downloadable HTML/browser tool with drumkits and any-length melodies, specifically saying Chrome Music Lab has been outgrown and existing tools are scale-bound.
An LMMS user requests an OpenUtau module and a pitch-adaptive drawing layer, explaining that directly drawing pitch would make expressive input more intuitive.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 requests point to the same gap: low-friction composition starts to break down when melodies and pitch expression become less elementary. Severity is high for learners because the workaround is a desktop DAW or several incompatible web toys.
current_workaround: Chrome Music Lab, scale-constrained sequencers, desktop DAWs, or manually exporting MIDI between tools.
incumbents_and_gap: Chrome Music Lab is approachable but limited; BandLab, LMMS, and OpenUtau are much heavier. The gap is a local-first browser sketchpad with unrestricted melody length and a simple pitch lane, not a full DAW.
smallest_useful_product: PWA with drum grid, free-pitch piano roll, one editable pitch curve, loop/export MIDI and a self-contained HTML share file. Non-goals: stems, VSTs, cloud accounts, AI composition, and multitrack mixing.
success_measure: At least 40% of first-time users create and export a 16-bar loop within 10 minutes; median time to first audible loop under 90 seconds.
monetization: free — distribution and trust matter more than paywalling a learner utility; optional donations can cover hosting.
constraints: Web Audio and Web MIDI support vary by browser; keep all audio local, require no copyrighted samples, and use CC0/original drum sounds.
why_distinct: It is not another prompt-to-song generator or full DAW: the product is deliberately a portable, unrestricted melody sketch surface.

title: Rhythm Pedal Tidy
user: Keyboard and e-kit players recording practice takes with sustain pedals who need a clean, playable MIDI capture instead of a tangle of overlapping notes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A drummer says Rock Band helped them practice form and timing through a MIDI-capable e-kit, while acknowledging the existing game experience was poor.
An LMMS user asks for pedal-recorded repeated notes to be mutually exclusive because release creates a messy set of overlaps that is hard to edit later.

recurrence: Independent practice and production users hit timing/input friction in 2026. It is acute because cleanup interrupts the feedback loop that makes instrument practice motivating.
current_workaround: Hand-edit overlapping piano-roll notes, avoid pedal capture, or tolerate inaccurate-looking takes.
incumbents_and_gap: DAWs can edit MIDI but bury cleanup in manual piano-roll work; rhythm games score performance but do not produce reusable MIDI. The gap is a one-click, explainable cleanup-and-replay practice tool.
smallest_useful_product: Offline Web MIDI recorder, sustain-aware de-overlap pass with before/after diff, tempo ramp, and replayable timing score. Non-goals: notation engraving, audio recording, subscriptions, and instrument lessons.
success_measure: 80% of recorded pedal passages need no manual cleanup after the suggested pass, measured by users accepting the output; 25% of users complete three takes in one session.
monetization: one-time — a modest desktop-like utility purchase fits a local practice tool with no service cost.
constraints: Web MIDI permission and Safari coverage require a clear fallback/import path; process recordings locally and do not transmit performance data.
why_distinct: Combines pedal-aware MIDI repair with a motivating practice loop rather than attempting to replace a DAW or a rhythm game.

title: Pad Light Choreographer
user: A MIDI-pad owner who wants hardware-first beat practice or tiny performances, with pad lights giving the next cue instead of a mouse-driven screen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A DJ-tool user says buttons and pads suit a text UI but knobs and faders are compromised, and explicitly calls for direct MIDI-controller support.
An LMMS musician describes basic expressive control as needlessly complex: vibrato is either track-wide or requires rapid pitch bends.

recurrence: The requests come from controller-oriented performers and DAW musicians in 2025–26, both frustrated by software that treats physical playing as an afterthought. Severity is medium-to-high because it blocks spontaneous practice.
current_workaround: Map pads manually in a DAW, run scripts, or use controller lights only for generic demos.
incumbents_and_gap: Ableton and hardware vendor apps are powerful but setup-heavy; web rhythm games rarely expose MIDI output. The gap is instant browser pairing plus reusable, visual pad cue patterns.
smallest_useful_product: Web MIDI PWA that discovers common grid pads, plays four-lane call-and-response patterns, lights target pads, and exports/imports compact JSON routines. Non-goals: DAW integration, commercial song charts, and device firmware flashing.
success_measure: 60% of supported-device visitors complete the connection test and play a first cue routine within five minutes; at least 30% save a routine.
monetization: free — hardware compatibility and community routine sharing are the adoption wedge; no backend is needed for v1.
constraints: Use only documented Web MIDI messages, test device mappings conservatively, and make unsupported hardware harmless; no copyrighted song content.
why_distinct: A cue-and-response instrument toy, not another piano-roll sequencer or a proprietary controller editor.

title: Session Layout Capsule
user: A home producer or live visualist who reopens a project and needs their auxiliary controls in the same spatial arrangement immediately.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A new Launchpad owner ended up writing a browser-based mini language just to sequence hardware lighting, showing how quickly a simple performance setup turns into custom tooling.
An LMMS report says instrument/effect windows lose both visibility and position after reopening a project, unlike the main editors.

recurrence: Two 2025–26 accounts show the same setup tax: creative sessions require an arrangement of small control surfaces, but that arrangement is not durable. Severity is medium but repeated every session.
current_workaround: Take screenshots, reopen and reposition windows manually, or write one-off scripts and configs.
incumbents_and_gap: Window managers and DAWs save some layout state, but neither captures a portable set of web tools, MIDI panels, notes, and named performance states. The gap is a shareable creative-session layout rather than OS automation.
smallest_useful_product: Local web dashboard that saves named layouts of tabs, MIDI cue panels, timers, and text notes; offers a restore checklist and a printable QR handoff. Non-goals: controlling arbitrary desktop windows, cloud sync, or DAW project parsing.
success_measure: Users restore a saved rehearsal layout in under two minutes and report fewer than two manual placement steps per restore in a five-session diary study.
monetization: free — a static local tool is more credible for rehearsal reliability and can build an audience for optional templates.
constraints: Browsers cannot reliably arrange external application windows, so v1 must be explicit about its checklist/launch-link boundary; store layouts locally by default.
why_distinct: It preserves a creative session's intent across lightweight tools, rather than pretending a browser can replace a window manager.

title: Web Audio Route Map
user: A browser-audio maker who needs to understand and share a small Web Audio signal chain without manually diagramming it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A project maker asks how to use an HTML techno machine and is actively looking for open-source, non-copyleft web-audio players.
An LMMS user asks for a minimap of the workstation because finding scattered Piano Roll and effect windows is slow and ambiguous.

recurrence: In 2026, web-audio adopters ask for usable building blocks while DAW users ask for a map of complex creative workspaces. The common pain is orientation, not sound generation.
current_workaround: Read source code, draw a diagram, use browser devtools, or keep a DAW patchbay and window layout open.
incumbents_and_gap: Tone.js and raw Web Audio are capable libraries, while DAWs have patchbays. None offers a tiny, embeddable route map that a browser-audio project can publish beside its controls.
smallest_useful_product: A dependency-free JS library plus demo that renders a live, keyboard-accessible node/route map from an explicit graph declaration and exports SVG. Non-goals: audio hosting, an audio engine, or automatic inspection of arbitrary minified code.
success_measure: Three independent makers add a map to a public Web Audio demo and new users correctly answer 4/5 signal-path questions in a usability test.
monetization: free — an open utility needs ecosystem adoption; paid support is possible only after proven use.
constraints: Do not claim complete automatic Web Audio introspection; emitted SVG must have text equivalents and no external telemetry.
why_distinct: A comprehension aid for open web-audio projects, not a DAW, player, or generative-music wrapper.

title: Frequency Feel
user: A beginner sound designer who wants to hear and see what a filter/EQ setting changes before committing it to a track or game effect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A metronome maker argues that timer-based implementations are wrong, underlining that seemingly basic audio tools have audible technical consequences.
A Godot user requests a graph for filter/EQ effects because dB descriptions do not make precise frequency behavior clear, including concern about uncomfortable headphone frequencies.

recurrence: Both 2026 sources point to a persistent learning failure: audio parameters are numeric but their outcomes are not legible. Severity is high where bad settings create discomfort or undermine timing.
current_workaround: Trial-and-error, external EQ charts, spectrum analyzers, and repeatedly rendering/listening to clips.
incumbents_and_gap: DAW analyzers and EQ plugins show advanced graphs but generally do not teach with controlled A/B examples; game-engine inspectors expose parameters with little auditory context. The gap is an interactive, local explainer.
smallest_useful_product: Offline interactive page with a safe synthetic sound, draggable filter/EQ controls, synchronized frequency response, before/after loudness-matched playback, and shareable parameter links. Non-goals: mastering, uploading user audio, medical/hearing claims, and AI mixing.
success_measure: In a five-question before/after test, 70% of first-time users correctly predict the direction of a filter change after using the tool for five minutes.
monetization: free — educational reach and embedding are more valuable than a paywall, and v1 has no operating cost.
constraints: Use conservative playback defaults, a visible volume warning, synthesized/original audio only, and no claims about preventing hearing damage.
why_distinct: It makes signal behavior tangible through controlled listening rather than being another generic visualizer or audio effect rack.

title: Mechanism Playground
user: A curious player or teacher who wants to assemble cams, gears, linkages, and levers into a small playable machine rather than merely watch an animation of one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: After viewing a collection of mechanical movements, a reader says they would love a game using the movements as building blocks and asks whether anything approaches it.
A game maker asks for random rotation and scale while drawing 2D nodes to place grass, rocks, and other repeated objects for visual evaluation.

recurrence: These adjacent 2026 requests converge on direct spatial experimentation: players want mechanisms as toys and creators need fast visual variation. Severity is medium but unusually well suited to a compact web product.
current_workaround: Watch mechanism videos, use heavyweight physics sandboxes, or hand-place and rotate repeated objects in an editor.
incumbents_and_gap: Algodoo and engineering simulators are broad and intimidating; construction games focus on progression rather than kinematic literacy. The gap is a friendly, bounded mechanism kit with short puzzle goals.
smallest_useful_product: Mobile-friendly 2D sandbox with ten kinematic primitives, snap points, a hand crank, slow motion, and ten local puzzle cards. Non-goals: realistic material stress, CAD export, multiplayer, and user-generated asset markets.
success_measure: 50% of visitors build a working crank-to-output chain in their first session; 20% complete three puzzle cards without a tutorial replay.
monetization: one-time — a polished educational toy can sell as a small purchase without collecting children’s data.
constraints: Use a deterministic, simplified kinematic model and make the age range clear; no user chat or data collection.
why_distinct: It centers recognisable mechanical movements as playful building vocabulary, not an open-ended physics clone or an engineering CAD package.

title: Pixel Tile Mask
user: A solo pixel-art game maker who needs collision, occlusion, and paint masks from a hand-drawn tile without tracing every irregular edge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A game creator discussing an RPG whose crafting is drawing pixel art reports building the visual/UI/animation layer alongside the game, illustrating the breadth of visual implementation work in small teams.
A Godot user says pixel-perfect occlusion/physics paint layers for complex pixel-art tiles are very tedious to draw and requests generation from the selected tile shape.

recurrence: A 2026 indie-creation account and a specific engine request describe the same maker burden: art creation expands into repetitive technical masking. Severity is high across tile-heavy games because the work repeats per tile and revision.
current_workaround: Trace collision/occlusion polygons manually in an engine, use rough rectangles, or write project-specific scripts.
incumbents_and_gap: Godot and Tiled support collision editing but not a focused, inspectable pixel-mask generation workflow. The gap is a browser utility that shows exactly what will export before it alters a project.
smallest_useful_product: Drag in PNG tile sheet, choose alpha/color threshold and simplification, preview collision and occlusion masks, then export Godot-compatible JSON/SVG. Non-goals: sprite generation, a level editor, cloud uploads, and auto-rigging.
success_measure: Users export an acceptable mask for 80% of a 20-tile test set with fewer than two manual edits per tile, compared with hand tracing baseline.
monetization: freemium — free single-sheet exports prove utility; a small one-time upgrade can unlock batch presets and engine formats.
constraints: Process art in-browser, preserve transparency, clearly state that generated masks need gameplay review, and avoid shipping third-party game assets.
why_distinct: It removes a narrow visual-to-technical handoff chore rather than trying to be an AI pixel-art generator or game engine.

title: Proof Motion Canvas
user: A teacher, explainer, or curious programmer who wants to turn a short argument into a clear, inspectable animated visual rather than a static slide deck or opaque video.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A reader wishes for a place where elegant algorithms can retain their visualized proof, arguing that presentation and proof are what keep a good idea from looking like a hack.
A game developer requests duration-based animation events because start/end frames and active windows are currently difficult to express and interruption can corrupt state.

recurrence: In 2026, both explanatory and interactive-animation creators need duration and state to be legible. Severity is high for educational material because a visual that cannot expose its timing is difficult to verify or reuse.
current_workaround: Slides, hand-edited video, custom code, or animation timelines that hide the underlying argument/state transitions.
incumbents_and_gap: Manim and motion-design apps are expressive but code-heavy or timeline-heavy; diagrams are static. The gap is a small declarative canvas where visual steps have named claims, start/end conditions, and a shareable replay.
smallest_useful_product: Static web editor for cards, arrows, numeric labels, and named timed intervals; playback has step controls and exports one self-contained HTML page. Non-goals: general video editing, AI proof generation, collaboration, and arbitrary scripting in v1.
success_measure: Five pilot explainers can create a replay with at least five inspectable steps in under 30 minutes, and peer viewers correctly restate the main invariant at a 70% rate.
monetization: free — shareable standalone explainers create distribution; no backend is necessary for the first useful version.
constraints: Keep math/content author-owned, label animations as explanations rather than formal verification, and provide accessible step text alongside motion.
why_distinct: It is a compact, inspectable explanation format—not an LLM-generated lesson, a generic whiteboard, or a full animation suite.

title: Co-op Boss Access
user: Friends running a quick shared-screen or multi-phone boss game who want cooperative roles and visual cues that remain understandable for players with depth-perception difficulty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A player asks for more collaborative mechanics in a tiny multiplayer dragon game, suggesting stackable damage boosts and shields that affect other players.
A platformer developer explains that vertically aligned drop shadows help players who struggle with depth perception, but current Godot workarounds are ugly or cumbersome.

recurrence: The 2025–26 evidence pairs a concrete co-op mechanics request with a concrete spatial-accessibility need. It is a valuable design gap because co-op games routinely make spatial clarity a visual afterthought.
current_workaround: Use simple damage races, rely on conventional shadows, or let less spatially confident players sit out demanding roles.
incumbents_and_gap: Party games offer co-op but rarely expose visual-accessibility modes beyond color settings; engine fixes do not make a playable design pattern. The gap is a demonstrated, reusable co-op interaction model where role cues are redundant and readable.
smallest_useful_product: A local-network browser boss game: one host screen, phones as two-button controllers, roles that charge shields/boosts for each other, optional high-contrast ground markers and motion reduction. Non-goals: accounts, matchmaking, chat, ads, and complex combat progression.
success_measure: In mixed-ability playtests, 80% of players can identify their role target and contribute an action within 30 seconds; average group completes a three-minute round without facilitator help.
monetization: free — a small accessible play prototype benefits from frictionless sharing; premium content is premature.
constraints: Use WebSockets only for room state, include clear privacy language for local-room codes, avoid collecting accessibility data, and test color/contrast independently of motion cues.
why_distinct: A concrete playable accessibility pattern for co-op, rather than a generic multiplayer template or an accessibility checklist.

title: Persistent Ink Cues
user: A presenter or workshop leader using a pen/tablet who needs an emphasis mark to persist until deliberately cleared, including on slow-refresh e-ink displays.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer porting Excalidraw to reMarkable says slow-refresh displays demand monotonic layouts and avoid self-initiated redraws that disrupt prior renders.
An Excalidraw user requests a persistent laser option because the current line fades after seconds and teaching/demos need emphasis to remain visible.

recurrence: A 2025 presenter request and a 2026 e-ink implementation report expose the same issue: transient drawing behavior is hostile to teaching and slow displays. Severity is high mid-presentation because the cue disappears exactly when viewers need it.
current_workaround: Draw permanent ink that must later be erased, repeatedly redraw a laser line, or use a separate slide annotation tool.
incumbents_and_gap: Excalidraw's laser is transient and whiteboards treat pen marks as permanent. The gap is a purpose-built cue layer with intentional persistence and minimal redraw semantics.
smallest_useful_product: Offline canvas overlay with transient, persistent-until-clear, and fade modes; big clear/undo controls; exported static frame; e-ink-safe reduced-animation mode. Non-goals: collaborative whiteboarding, cloud documents, OCR, and slide hosting.
success_measure: In a five-minute mock lesson, presenters use a persistent cue without needing to redraw it, and e-ink users report no involuntary redraw during a one-minute idle period.
monetization: one-time — a dependable presentation utility has a clear individual value and no recurring service requirement.
constraints: Must be usable with pointer, touch, and keyboard; local-only storage; avoid claims of official reMarkable support unless tested on hardware.
why_distinct: A cue layer optimized for persistence and slow displays, not a general-purpose whiteboard clone.

title: Stream Access Cues
user: A blind or keyboard-first independent streamer who needs a reliable local cue surface for stream metadata, scenes, and timing without inaccessible embedded web controls.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker of an on-device reading app says streaming was the hardest part because interactive use cannot wait for an entire paragraph's audio before response.
A blind OBS/NVDA user cannot set Twitch title or category because its embedded web dock is unreachable, while YouTube's native dialog works; they propose a native dialog or focusable dock.

recurrence: The 2026 reports share a harsh real-time constraint: feedback/control that waits on inaccessible or delayed UI is not usable in a live setting. Severity is critical for a solo streamer who cannot independently set metadata.
current_workaround: Ask another person to configure stream information, fight embedded browser controls, or switch platforms/workflows.
incumbents_and_gap: OBS has rich controls but depends on platform docks; Twitch's web UI and generic macro pads are not a focused accessible workflow. The gap is a screen-reader-first local cue dashboard that controls only well-supported APIs.
smallest_useful_product: Keyboard-first local web dashboard using OBS WebSocket for named scene/cue actions, an editable spoken checklist, and launch links to platform metadata pages. Non-goals: bypassing Twitch UI, storing OAuth tokens in a hosted service, streaming video, or replacing OBS.
success_measure: A blind keyboard-only tester completes a pre-stream checklist and changes an OBS scene without sighted assistance; 90% of controls have clear screen-reader names and documented shortcuts.
monetization: free — accessibility tooling needs broad testing and trust; a local-first open core avoids making independent streaming a paid privilege.
constraints: Do not promise Twitch metadata writes unless the current authorized API supports them; keep OBS credentials local, meet WCAG keyboard/name requirements, and test with NVDA.
why_distinct: It narrows to independent, accessible live control instead of building another streaming platform, chatbot, or visual macro deck.
